paragraphs: If we ask what exactly the greatest good of all is, the good every system of legislation should aim at, we will find that it comes down to two main things: liberty and equality. Liberty, because every particular dependence removes that much force from the body of the State; and equality, because liberty cannot exist without it.

I have already defined civil liberty. By equality we should understand not that power and wealth must be exactly the same for everyone, but that power should never be great enough for violence and should always be exercised through rank and law; and that, as for wealth, no citizen should be rich enough to buy another, and none so poor that he is forced to sell himself:[1] which means that the great must show moderation in goods and position, and the common sort must show moderation in greed and covetousness.

People tell us that such equality is an impractical ideal that cannot really exist. But if it will inevitably be abused, does it follow that we should not at least regulate it? Precisely because the force of circumstances constantly tends to destroy equality, the force of legislation should always tend to maintain it.

These general aims of every good legislative system must be adapted in each country to its local situation and to the temperament of its inhabitants. These circumstances should decide, in each case, which particular system of institutions is best, perhaps not in itself, but for the State it is meant for. If the soil is barren and unproductive, or the country too crowded for its inhabitants, the people should turn to industry and the crafts, and trade what they make for the goods they lack. If instead a people lives on rich plains and fertile slopes, or, in a good land, has too few inhabitants, it should give all its attention to agriculture, which makes people multiply, and should drive out the crafts, which would only depopulate the country by gathering the few inhabitants there are into a few places.[2] If a nation lives on a long and convenient coastline, let it cover the sea with ships and foster commerce and navigation. Its life will be short and glorious. If the sea on its coasts washes against nothing but almost inaccessible rocks, let it remain barbarous and live on fish. Its life will be quieter, perhaps better, and certainly happier. In a word, besides the principles all nations share, every nation has something in itself that gives them a particular application and makes its legislation distinctively its own. So among the Jews long ago, and more recently among the Arabs, the chief object was religion; among the Athenians, letters; at Carthage and Tyre, commerce; at Rhodes, shipping; at Sparta, war; at Rome, virtue. The author of _The Spirit of the Laws_ has shown with many examples the art by which the legislator steers the constitution toward each of these objects.

What makes a State’s constitution truly solid and lasting is careful respect for what is fitting, so that natural relations and the laws always agree on every point, and law only serves, so to speak, to secure, accompany and correct those relations. But suppose the legislator mistakes his object and adopts a principle other than the one circumstances naturally point to. Suppose his principle makes for servitude where they make for liberty, or for wealth where they make for a large population, or for peace where they make for conquest. Then the laws will insensibly lose their influence, the constitution will change, and the State will have no rest from trouble until it is either destroyed or changed, and nature has resumed her invincible sway.
